title: From Titans to Technocrats
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn uses Columbus, Ohio's K-shaped economic trajectory as a case study in the failure of contemporary civic leadership, arguing that the city's economic growth has been captured by an increasingly narrow professional class (Technocrats) while the working-class majority has been left behind, and that the civic leaders who should address this gap have neither the roots nor the will to do so. The piece traces the historical shift from 'Titan' civic leadership -- the locally-rooted business magnates who built institutions, funded public goods, and identified their personal fortunes with the health of the whole city -- to 'Technocrat' civic leadership: the mobile professional class that chooses cities based on amenity optimization, participates in civic life as a consumer rather than an investor, and has no structural reason to care about the bottom half of the local economy. Renn argues this is not a Columbus-specific problem but a nationwide pattern that makes addressing urban inequality structurally much harder than it would have been in the Titan era.
points: * The shift from Titan to Technocrat civic leadership represents a fundamental change in the structural relationship between civic leaders and the health of the communities they lead: Titans' personal wealth was tied to local institutional health; Technocrats' wealth is mobile and nationally determined. * Columbus's K-shaped economy (strong professional sector, stagnant working-class outcomes) is not the result of policy failure alone but of a civic leadership vacuum: the class that would historically have advocated for balanced growth no longer has structural incentives to do so. * Technocrat civic leaders participate in civic life as consumers (choosing amenities, supporting causes) rather than investors (building institutions, absorbing risk for the common good) -- a fundamental change in the nature of civic engagement. * The Titan era was not without problems -- concentrated power, exclusion, paternalism -- but it produced durable local institutions (hospitals, universities, libraries, parks) that were built with local capital for local benefit and that persist long after the Titans are gone. * Addressing urban inequality requires the kind of long-term, locally-rooted investment that the Technocrat class is structurally unlikely to make -- making the problem harder to solve with each passing decade as the Titan generation ages out.
quotes: Columbus has one of the strongest economic growth records of any large American city over the past two decades. It also has some of the worst economic mobility outcomes. Those two facts are not in tension. They are the same fact from two different angles.

The Titan was rooted. His family was from here. His bank was here. His factories were here. His children would live here after he died. When he gave money to build a hospital, he was betting on the community he would spend his entire life in. That bet is what the Technocrat does not make.

The Technocrat chose Columbus the way he might choose a hotel. The amenities were excellent, the cost-to-quality ratio was favorable, and he could always leave if something better came along. This is not a criticism of the Technocrat as a person. It is a description of the structural relationship he has to the place.

Civic capacity is not primarily a policy problem. It is a class structure problem. You need a class of people who are locally rooted enough to absorb the long time horizons and uncertain returns of institution-building. Technocrats, structurally, are not that class. They are optimized for mobility and optionality, which are the enemies of the civic patience that cities need.

The institutions that still function well in Columbus -- the major hospital systems, the university, the arts infrastructure -- were mostly built in the Titan era. They are spending down the civic capital of a class that no longer exists in its original form. What happens when the spending is done is the question I cannot answer.
